walkthroughs.h2: From Wegener to Modern Plate Tectonics
walkthroughs.body_html: Alfred Wegener proposed continental drift in 1912, supported by fit of coastlines, fossils (Mesosaurus, Glossopteris), and geology. He lacked a mechanism. Mid-twentieth century evidence resolved this: Holmes' mantle convection, palaeomagnetic striping at the Mid-Atlantic Ridge (Vine and Matthews, 1963), and seafloor age data confirmed sea-floor spreading. The unified plate tectonics theory emerged ~1968.

Convergent: oceanic subducts beneath continental, forming Andes-type arcs (Nazca-South American) and andesitic stratovolcanoes; continental-continental collision builds the Himalayas (Indian-Eurasian, ~5 cm/yr). Divergent: mid-ocean ridges (Mid-Atlantic, ~2.5 cm/yr) and continental rifts (East African Rift). Transform: San Andreas Fault (~3.5 cm/yr) generates large earthquakes (1906 San Francisco M7.9, 1989 Loma Prieta M6.9).

Approximately 5% of volcanism occurs at hotspots over stationary mantle plumes. The Pacific Plate moves NW over the Hawaiian hotspot at ~9 cm/yr, generating a chain from Kilauea (active) through Maui, Oahu, Kauai, then the Emperor Seamounts. Iceland sits over a plume coincident with the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, producing exceptional basaltic output (Eyjafjallajokull 2010, Fagradalsfjall 2021-23, Sundhnukur 2024).
